title: Next.js Auth Handbook: Sessions, Middleware and the Data Access Layer
summary: Quick revision notes on session vs JWT cookie auth in Next.js, protecting routes with middleware, verifying auth in Server Components and Server Actions, the data access layer pattern, Auth.js basics, and why middleware alone is not enough.

chapters.title: Sessions vs JWT Cookies
points: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do. Auth flow is: credentials, create session, store in cookie, verify on every request
Database session: cookie holds only an opaque session ID; the server looks up the row on each request, so it can be revoked instantly but costs a DB hit
Stateless JWT session: cookie holds a signed (and optionally encrypted) token with claims such as userId and expiresAt; verification is a signature check with no DB call
Comparison: DB session = easy revocation, slower, more storage; JWT = fast and scalable, hard to revoke before expiry, so keep it short-lived and keep payload small (no secrets)

Cookie flags to set: httpOnly (no JS access), secure (HTTPS only), sameSite=lax (CSRF mitigation), path=/, and an expires matching the session; set via cookies().set() in a Server Action or Route Handler
Common mistake: storing a JWT in localStorage (readable by XSS) or putting sensitive data in an unencrypted payload (a JWT is signed, not hidden)

chapters.title: Protecting Routes in Middleware
points: Middleware runs before a request completes, so it is the fast first gate for redirecting unauthenticated users; in newer Next.js versions the file may be named proxy.ts, so check the version docs in node_modules/next/dist/docs
Pattern: read the session cookie from req.cookies, decrypt or verify it, then NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/login', req.nextUrl)) when a protected path has no valid session
Define protectedRoutes and publicRoutes arrays and compare against req.nextUrl.pathname; also redirect a logged-in user away from /login to the dashboard
export const config = { matcher: ['/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|.*\.png$).*)'] } excludes static assets and avoids running on every file request
Middleware must stay cheap: do optimistic checks only (cookie decrypt or JWT verify), never DB queries, and avoid Node-only APIs because it may run on the Edge runtime

chapters.title: Auth in Server Components and Actions
points: Server Components cannot set cookies or redirect after streaming starts; read the session with cookies() (async in recent versions, so await it) and call redirect('/login') from next/navigation when missing
Layouts do not re-render on client navigation (partial rendering), so an auth check placed only in a layout can be skipped; check in every page or in the data fetch itself
Server Actions are public POST endpoints: anyone can call them directly with fetch, so verify the session and authorization inside every action, not just where the form is shown
Example action: async function deletePost(id) { 'use server'; const session = await verifySession(); if (!session) throw new Error('Unauthorized'); check ownership or role, then mutate }
Validate action inputs (e.g. with Zod) and never trust hidden form fields or client-sent userId; derive the user from the session instead

chapters.title: The Data Access Layer Pattern
points: Data Access Layer (DAL) is a server-only module where every database read and write lives, and each function performs its own auth and authorization check before touching data
Put import 'server-only' at the top so the module fails the build if a Client Component imports it
verifySession wrapped in React cache() dedupes the cookie decrypt and DB lookup to once per render pass: export const verifySession = cache(async () => { ... redirect('/login') ... })

Return DTOs (Data Transfer Objects) with only the fields the caller may see, e.g. return admins the full row but others just { name }, so secrets like passwordHash or email never leak into props sent to the client
Comparison: scattered checks in components are easy to forget; a DAL gives one auditable place, and components and actions call getUser() or getPost(id) instead of querying the DB directly

chapters.title: Auth.js Basics and Why Middleware Is Not Enough
points: Auth.js (NextAuth v5) setup: export const { handlers, auth, signIn, signOut } = NextAuth({ providers: [...] }) in auth.ts; expose handlers via app/api/auth/[...nextauth]/route.ts as export const { GET, POST } = handlers

Providers: OAuth (GitHub, Google) or Credentials; the Credentials provider forces the JWT session strategy, while an adapter (Prisma, Drizzle) enables database sessions with session: { strategy: 'database' }
Read the session anywhere on the server with const session = await auth(); trigger login and logout with signIn('github') and signOut() inside Server Actions; set AUTH_SECRET in the env
Callbacks: jwt and session callbacks copy custom fields like id or role onto the token and session; the authorized callback can be used for middleware gating

Middleware alone is not enough: it is optimistic and path-based, so matcher mistakes, renamed routes, direct Server Action POSTs, and the 2025 middleware-bypass CVE (x-middleware-subrequest header) can skip it; always re-verify in the DAL as the real security boundary
Defense in depth rule: middleware for redirects and UX, DAL checks for security, and keep Next.js patched

chapters.title: Auth Cheat Sheet
points: Session choice: DB session for revocation, JWT cookie for stateless speed; flags httpOnly + secure + sameSite=lax
Middleware: optimistic cookie check, redirect to /login, matcher excludes _next and static files, no DB calls
Every Server Component data fetch, Server Action and Route Handler must verify the session itself; actions are public endpoints
DAL checklist: 'server-only', cache(verifySession), authorize inside each function, return DTOs not raw rows
Auth.js: auth() to read session, signIn()/signOut() in actions, AUTH_SECRET required, callbacks jwt then session to add role
Rule of thumb: middleware = UX gate, DAL = security gate; never rely on middleware alone
